newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Zedillo attacks foreign meddling.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Zedillo attacks foreign meddling.

text.p: Stung by U.S. criticism of Mexico's anti-drug efforts, President Ernesto Zedillo attacked foreign interference in his country on Tuesday and hailed the government-run oil monopoly as a "bulwark" of Mexican sovereignty.

Under pressure to take a tougher line with Washington since the House of Representatives voted to censure Mexico for drug corruption last week, Zedillo used the anniversary of Mexico's 1938 expropriation of the oil industry from foreign companies to launch a strong nationalist attack.
"In no way will we accept that the sovereignty and dignity of Mexico be an instrument of foreign political interests," Zedillo told a crowd including local oil workers.
"Our sovereignty does not recognise submission to any foreign power," he declared in a stern tone.

Although politicians in Washington said the Senate was likely to tone down the House's censure of Mexico's anti-drug efforts when it debates the issue, Mexicans were enraged by the public discussion in the United States of their drug performance.

Mexican officials say they deserve applause rather than reproach from Washington for attacking drug corruption. They also resent criticism of their efforts to fight a trade they say exists mainly to satisfy the craving of U.S. drug users.
Using the typically coded language of Mexican politics, Zedillo did not mention the drug issue by name in his address at the oil refining town of Cadereyta, 400 miles (640 km) north of Mexico City.
But, in a clear reference to the row over whether the United States would "certify" (approve) Mexico as a reliable drug war ally, he said:

"Under no circumstances will we Mexicans accept that domestic conflicts of interests of other countries undermine our sovereignty and in no way will we accept that legal acts derived from these conflicts interfere in the internal affairs of our country."
Oil union members cheered Zedillo on, waving a huge multi-coloured banner that read:
"In 1938 Mexico was "decertified" because it expropriated its oil and it won through. Today...in 1997 we were "decertified" for defending our dignity and sovereignty."

President Bill Clinton announced on Feb. 28 that he would grant full drug certification to Mexico but some congressmen have since been trying to reverse the ruling, arguing that massive corruption in Mexico meant the country did not deserve the official seal of approval.

Departing Tuesday from his habitual free-market speeches in favour of foreign investment and economic deregulation, Zedillo praised the state oil monopoly Pemex as a "symbol of our historical struggles for sovereignty".
In his first two years of government from 1994-1996, Zedillo pinned his colours to the masthead of privatisation, deregulation and free markets.

Only last year he had attempted to sell off some Pemex petrochemical plants to foreigners but backed down in the face of fierce union opposition, agreeing instead to allow foreigners a maximum 49 percent stake in certain plants only.

Political analysts say Zedillo has now been obliged to change his message -- at least temporarily -- because of the rising tide of anti-American sentiment caused by the Washington congressional debate.
The 1938 expropriation of the Mexican oil industry by then president Lazaro Cardenas infuriated the U.S. government and the British oil industry but was hugely popular with Mexicans.
